analysis.one_liner: Bars TV and print ads for new prescription drugs during their first three years on the market.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and died when the Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped drug companies from advertising new prescription drugs directly to consumers for three years after FDA approval, unless the Health Secretary found the ads would help public health. It also would have made side-effect and risk information in ads appear in larger, more prominent type, allowed the government to force label changes after approval, imposed civil fines starting at $250,000 for violating ad rules, and funded an FDA education campaign about drug risks.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers would get three years of safety experience with a new drug before seeing ads urging them to ask their doctor for it, since rare or long-term side effects often only surface after a drug is widely used. Patients taking advertised drugs would see clearer, more prominent warnings in ads. Doctors would face less pressure from patients requesting heavily advertised new drugs, and the FDA would get $2.5 million a year to police drug ads.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and consumers of prescription drugs

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits direct-to-consumer advertising of a prescription drug for the first three years after FDA approval, with a waiver if the Secretary finds the advertising would have affirmative value to public health, and allows an extension of the ban if post-approval studies show significant adverse health effects.
Requires side effect, contraindication, and effectiveness information in drug ads to be prominently displayed in font size and location set by regulation.

Imposes civil penalties of up to $250,000 for a first violation of drug advertising rules, doubling for repeat violations, with each distribution of a violative ad a separate offense, and allows the Secretary to order corrective advertising.

Lets the Secretary require labeling changes after approval to ensure safe and effective use, order manufacturers to notify the public and doctors, and funds a public education campaign on drug risks, including $2.5 million per year to FDA for fiscal 2007 and 2008.

analysis.who_pays: Drug manufacturers would lose the ability to build consumer demand for new drugs immediately after approval, during the years when advertising typically drives the fastest sales growth. Broadcasters, magazines, and advertising agencies would lose a large stream of pharmaceutical ad revenue. Companies could also face civil fines and mandated corrective ads.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers and media ad sellers

drawbacks.text: A three-year advertising ban would delay information about genuinely new treatments reaching patients who might benefit, and the waiver process gives the Health Secretary discretion that could be applied inconsistently.

Consumer advertising also carries health information to people who do not see doctors regularly; the bill addresses this with a public education campaign but critics argued direct ads help patients discuss conditions with physicians.
Civil penalties doubling with each violation, with every ad distribution a separate offense, could expose manufacturers to very large cumulative fines.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is giving regulators and doctors time to learn a new drug's real-world risks before mass consumer marketing amplifies demand. The main cost is slower awareness of new treatments and a reduction in pharmaceutical ad revenue that broadcasters and publishers depend on. Whether the trade is worth it depends largely on how often new drugs turn out to have serious side effects discovered after approval, which is exactly what this kind of waiting period is meant to reveal.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in September 2005 and then to its Health subcommittee a few weeks later, and neither ever acted on it; it died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on September 29, 2005, with Rep. Jo Ann Emerson as the other original sponsor, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
On October 17, 2005, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, which is the last action recorded for it.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded, and the bill was never enacted before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical companies kept the ability to advertise new prescription drugs to consumers immediately after FDA approval, and the broadcasters and publishers that sell that advertising kept the revenue. Consumers got no change in how new drugs are marketed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug companies and their ad buyers

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban direct-to-consumer drug advertising for three years after approval and strengthen ad safety rules.

for.name: Rep. Jo Ann Emerson
for.what_they_did: Joined DeLauro in introducing the bill as its Republican cosponsor.

for.name: 8 House Democrats, 1 House Republican, and 1 Independent cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan backing from 10 members total.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Joe Barton (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the rest of the 109th Congress, leaving it in the Health subcommittee until the Congress expired.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's small sponsorship was bipartisan — 8 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 1 Independent cosponsor — but the committee that buried it was controlled by Republicans, and no vote was ever recorded to measure broader support.

industries.note: The bill would have barred them from advertising new drugs to consumers for three years after approval and subjected their promotion to civil fines up to $250,000 and corrective-ad orders. Consumer ads are a major tool for driving early prescription volume, so the bill targeted exactly the practice that builds new-drug sales fastest.

Drug advertising is one of the largest sources of TV and magazine ad revenue; a three-year moratorium on new-drug ads and stricter prominence rules for risk disclosures would have cut that revenue. The industry's interest in maximizing ad volume ran against the bill's goal of reducing promotional pressure before a drug's risks are known.
